q-10510:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the ball is $u=0\,\text{m/s}.$

- The ball covers the distance of $s=44.1\,\text{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $t,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\ 44.1 & =(0)t+\frac{1}{2}(9.8){t}^{2} \\ 44.1 & =4.9{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{44.1}{4.9} \\ {t}^{2} & =9 \\ t & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the ball hits the ground after $t=3$ seconds.

q-135228:
To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the marble is $u=24.5\,\text{m/s}.$

- The marble covers the distance of $s=245\,\text{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $t,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\ 245 & =(24.5)t+\frac{1}{2}(9.8){t}^{2} \\ 245 & =24.5t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 50(4.9) & =5(4.9)t+4.9{t}^{2} \\ 50\cancel{(4.9)} & =5\cancel{(4.9)}t+\cancel{(4.9)}{t}^{2} \\ 50 & =5t+{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2}+5t-50 & =0 \\ (t+10)(t-5) & =0 \\ t & =-10,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the marble hits the ground after $t=5$ seconds.

q-120657:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1}=\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify our expression by factoring the numerator as a difference of squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1} & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1)(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1)\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)}}{\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)}} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1}=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1.
$$
